source.authors: Anderson JM, Clegg TM, Véras LVMVQ, Holland KN
source.title: Insight into shark magnetic field perception from empirical observations

value: conditioned sharks made significantly more approaches to the target during stimulus activation (S+) than before or after activation (S-), p < 0.01
method: behavioural: conditioned approach to a food target during a coil-generated magnetic stimulus, S+ against S- periods
conditions: Captive sandbar sharks in a 7 m diameter circular tank, conditioned with a food reward to seek a target when a magnetic stimulus (coil of 18 AWG copper wire around the tank) was on; stimulus intensities 0.03 to 2.89 microtesla; unimpaired series 10 trials with 5 sharks in the first eight and 7 in the last two
quote: Sharks in the study demonstrated strong responses to magnetic stimuli, making significantly more approaches to the target (p = < 0.01) during stimulus activation (S+) than before or after activation (S−).
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0; full text read on the publisher's own free copy (link.springer.com, Scientific Reports). Name: ACCEPTED, exact match in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv (GBIF usage key 2418009). The Results give Friedman chi-squared 61.417, df = 20, p = 2.99e-06 and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test p = 0.001953 for passes over the target in the S+ minute against any other one-minute bin. The authors state the likelihood that transient electrical artefacts were the stimulus was low, but they did not identify the receptor.

source.authors: Anderson JM, Clegg TM, Véras LVMVQ, Holland KN
source.title: Insight into shark magnetic field perception from empirical observations

value: sharks with reversible magnetosensory impairment were less capable of discriminating changes to the local magnetic field; no difference in approaches to the target between S+ and S- (p = 0.375)
method: behavioural: same conditioned-approach test after neodymium magnets were glued over the olfactory capsules to impair magnetoreception
conditions: Impairment: neodymium magnets 1.2 x 0.3 x 0.3 cm sealed in gelatine-filled plastic boxes, glued to the dorsal skin over the olfactory capsules; 10 impaired trials, 4 sharks in seven trials and 3 in the remaining three; no empty-box (sham) control trials were conducted, the authors relied on impaired sharks swimming and feeding normally and responding to stronger stimuli; same tank and coil as the unimpaired series
quote: Sharks exposed to reversible magnetosensory impairment were less capable of discriminating changes to the local magnetic field, with no difference seen in approaches to the target under the S+ and S− conditions (p = 0.375).
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0; full text read on the publisher's own free copy (link.springer.com, Scientific Reports). Name: ACCEPTED, exact match in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv (GBIF usage key 2418009). Contrary/null result: loss of the S+ versus S- difference after impairment. Absence of a sham-magnet control means the effect of the box or the attached weight is not separated from the effect of the magnetic field. The authors infer that magnetic perception in sharks is not solely electrosensory and that putative magnetoreceptors may lie in the naso-olfactory capsules (inference in the Abstract, not a direct test of the capsules).

source.authors: Anderson JM, Clegg TM, Véras LVMVQ, Holland KN
source.title: Insight into shark magnetic field perception from empirical observations

value: 100% conditioned response in all unimpaired sharks to every applied field intensity, 0.03 to 2.89 microtesla
method: behavioural: conditioned approach to a food target during a coil-generated magnetic stimulus; intensities used in training and conditioning
conditions: Captive sandbar sharks in a 7 m diameter circular tank, conditioned with a food reward to seek a target when a magnetic stimulus (coil of 18 AWG copper wire around the tank) was on; stimulus intensities 0.03 to 2.89 microtesla; unimpaired series 10 trials with 5 sharks in the first eight and 7 in the last two
quote: Unimpaired, conditioned sharks produced a 100% response (all sharks demonstrating a conditioned response) to all applied magnetic field intensities used in training and conditioning, which ranged from 0.03 to 2.89 micro-Tesla (μT).
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0; full text read on the publisher's own free copy (link.springer.com, Scientific Reports). Name: ACCEPTED, exact match in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv (GBIF usage key 2418009). 0.03 microtesla was the weakest field applied, so the sentence gives no detection limit below it. The Abstract says the paper quantifies transient electrical artefacts and finds it unlikely they served as the stimulus; those figures were not logged.

source.authors: Desai R, Garratt MA, Srinivasan MV, Ravi S
source.title: Effects of object motion on visual acuity in honeybees

value: stationary targets: change in shape (disc vs diamond) perceived only for targets subtending visual angles above 1.9 degrees
method: behavioural: Y-maze choice after training, stationary disc against diamond at four sizes
conditions: Y-maze binary choice: foragers trained to a stimulus on a sugar-solution feeder, then tested with empty nectaries; stimuli (disc vs diamond) 3D-printed from one PETG filament spool; sizes 3.1, 1.9, 0.88 and 0.44 degrees; N = 50 bees per size (five sets of 10); moving stimuli oscillated side to side at +/-20 degrees and 3.5 Hz; viewing distance not stated; no contrast or brightness measurements reported
quote: When stimuli were stationary, bees perceived the change in shape only for targets that subtended visual angles >1.9°.
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0 (issued 2026-04-15); full text read on the publisher's own free PDF (journals.biologists.com). Name: ACCEPTED in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. The Abstract says '>1.9°', but the Results table gives significant discrimination at 1.9 degrees (chi-squared p = 0.0232, binomial p = 0.0153) as well as 3.1 degrees (p = 0.0007; 0.0003) and none at 0.88 degrees (p = 0.1491; 0.1189) or 0.44 degrees (p = 0.3818; 0.1611), so the stationary threshold lies between 0.88 and 1.9 degrees on the Results. The authors report angular size, not cycles per degree, so no acuity_cpd is computed.

source.authors: Desai R, Garratt MA, Srinivasan MV, Ravi S
source.title: Effects of object motion on visual acuity in honeybees

value: moving stimulus preferred over a stationary one at every size tested, down to 0.44 degrees
method: behavioural: Y-maze choice, stationary against moving stimulus
conditions: Y-maze binary choice: foragers trained to a stimulus on a sugar-solution feeder, then tested with empty nectaries; stimuli (disc vs diamond) 3D-printed from one PETG filament spool; sizes 3.1, 1.9, 0.88 and 0.44 degrees; N = 50 bees per size (five sets of 10); moving stimuli oscillated side to side at +/-20 degrees and 3.5 Hz; viewing distance not stated; no contrast or brightness measurements reported
quote: However, when presented with a stationary and a moving stimulus, they consistently preferred the moving stimulus, even when both stimuli subtended angles as small as 0.44°.
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0 (issued 2026-04-15); full text read on the publisher's own free PDF (journals.biologists.com). Name: ACCEPTED in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. The authors also report that motion cues override a learned preference for a familiar stationary shape (Abstract). Motion was produced by servo-driven oscillation; the Discussion gives peak angular velocities up to 500 deg/s and averages near 350 deg/s. Stimuli were shape-matched in material but contrast and brightness were not measured, so a luminance-flicker cue from the moving target cannot be excluded.

source.authors: Desai R, Garratt MA, Srinivasan MV, Ravi S
source.title: Effects of object motion on visual acuity in honeybees

value: disc and diamond discriminated at 0.44 degrees when both targets moved, not when both were stationary
method: behavioural: Y-maze choice, shape discrimination with both targets moving against both stationary
conditions: Y-maze binary choice: foragers trained to a stimulus on a sugar-solution feeder, then tested with empty nectaries; stimuli (disc vs diamond) 3D-printed from one PETG filament spool; sizes 3.1, 1.9, 0.88 and 0.44 degrees; N = 50 bees per size (five sets of 10); moving stimuli oscillated side to side at +/-20 degrees and 3.5 Hz; viewing distance not stated; no contrast or brightness measurements reported
quote: Most notably, bees successfully discriminated shapes at the smallest tested size of 0.44° when both targets were in motion, but not when they were stationary.
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0 (issued 2026-04-15); full text read on the publisher's own free PDF (journals.biologists.com). Name: ACCEPTED in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. Results: with both targets moving, the trained diamond was preferred 70% at 3.1 degrees and 72% at 0.44 degrees (N = 50 per size). The paper concludes that motion enhances acuity beyond earlier stationary-target limits; it tests only 0.44 degrees as the smallest size, so the lower bound for moving targets is not found.

method: grating acuity as reported by the review from New and Bull (2011); the review does not state how the 7.3 value was obtained (it describes anatomical estimation of grating acuity in general terms)

source.title: Lizard visual ecology
source.journal: Frontiers in Amphibian and Reptile Science 2: 1426675

where: Section 3.2, Spatial acuity of the retina
quote: The sleepy lizard Tiliqua rugosa, a slow-moving animal that feeds on vegetation and slow-moving prey has a value of 7.3 cycles per degree (New and Bull, 2011).
note: Review article, graded by what it reports for one named species; the primary paper (New and Bull 2011) was not opened. Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0; full text read on the publisher's own page (frontiersin.org). Name: ACCEPTED, exact match in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv (GBIF usage key 2462522). The review ranks Ctenophorus species (20-26 cpd) and Anolis carolinensis (12-14 cpd) above this value; those sentences are over 40 words and were not filed.
